question: What is energy security? Discuss India's energy mix and the policy measures to achieve energy security and clean energy transition.
why: Energy needs, resources, policy and security are listed in the 2026 syllabus; energy is the second-most asked theme (24 questions).
intro: Energy security is the uninterrupted availability of energy at affordable prices and with acceptable environmental impact. India imports about four-fifths of its oil and a large part of its gas, which makes security a strategic concern.

pts: Coal remains the main source of electricity; oil and gas for transport and industry; growing renewables (solar, wind, small hydro, biomass) and nuclear.
Per capita energy use is low; demand will rise with growth.
Renewable targets (500 GW non-fossil by 2030), National Solar Mission, wind-solar hybrid policy, green hydrogen mission, ethanol blending, PM-KUSUM and Surya Ghar rooftops.
Energy efficiency: PAT scheme, BEE star labelling, UJALA LED programme, Energy Conservation Act.
Diversification: strategic petroleum reserves, overseas assets, international solar alliance, cross-border grids, nuclear expansion.
Import dependence, discom finances, storage and transmission gaps, price volatility and just-transition concerns for coal regions.

conclusion: Energy security today means a diversified and cleaner mix with efficient use. Domestic renewables and storage are the surest hedge against import risk.

theme: Environment Impact Assessment and environmental legislation
question: Explain the process of Environment Impact Assessment in India and evaluate its effectiveness. Mention the main environmental laws that govern it.
why: EIA is a named syllabus item in two places (item 5 and environmental legislation in item 6); asked repeatedly in the compilation.
intro: EIA is a systematic process to predict the environmental effects of a project before approval so that damage can be avoided or minimised. In India it is governed by the EIA Notification 2006 issued under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986.

pts: Screening (Category A and B projects), scoping with terms of reference, baseline data and impact prediction, public consultation and hearing, appraisal by expert committees, grant of environmental clearance with conditions, and monitoring.

Environment (Protection) Act 1986, Air and Water Acts, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, Wildlife Protection Act 1972, Biological Diversity Act 2002, National Green Tribunal Act 2010, CRZ and international conventions (Montreal, Kyoto, CITES, UNFCCC).
Strengths: public participation, conditions on projects, NGT review.
Weaknesses: poor quality of reports by consultants, weak monitoring, ex-post clearances, exemptions in draft notifications, limited cumulative impact assessment.
Independent accredited assessors, strong public hearings, digital compliance monitoring, strategic and cumulative assessment.

conclusion: EIA balances development and conservation only if it is credible. Independent assessment and strict follow-up make it effective.

theme: Water resources, watershed management and soil conservation
question: Discuss the importance of watershed management for water and soil conservation in India with special reference to the drought-prone areas of Andhra Pradesh.
why: Water resources, watershed management, soil reclamation, coastal and soil erosion are separate syllabus lines; Rayalaseema gives the AP context.
intro: A watershed is the area from which rainfall drains to a common point. Managing it conserves soil and water, recharges groundwater and supports rain-fed agriculture, which covers over half of India's cropped area.

pts: Soil and moisture conservation: contour bunds, terraces, check dams, farm ponds, gully plugging; vegetative measures such as agroforestry and grass cover.
Water harvesting and groundwater recharge; community participation through user groups.
Integrated Watershed Management Programme under PMKSY (Watershed Development component), National Watershed Development Project for Rainfed Areas, Neeru-Chettu (AP) and MGNREGS works.
Rayalaseema's low and erratic rainfall, red and black soils prone to erosion, falling groundwater; watershed work and farm ponds improve drought-proofing.
Maintenance, equity in sharing benefits and weak convergence; need for scientific planning with remote sensing.

conclusion: Watershed management is the base of drought-proofing and sustainable farming. Community ownership keeps the structures working beyond project life.

theme: Human diseases: tuberculosis, malaria and HIV
question: Describe the causative agents, transmission, symptoms and preventive measures of tuberculosis and malaria. Mention the national programmes to control them.
why: Infectious diseases are asked 23 times, mostly as the 'agent, transmission, symptoms and control' form; TB, malaria, HIV and cholera are named in the syllabus.
intro: Tuberculosis and malaria are major infectious diseases of India. TB is caused by a bacterium and malaria by a protozoan parasite; both are preventable and curable.

pts: Agent: Mycobacterium tuberculosis; spread by droplets from pulmonary cases; symptoms: cough over two weeks, fever, weight loss, night sweats.
Diagnosis: sputum smear, CBNAAT/Truenat; treatment: DOTS with multi-drug regimen; MDR-TB and XDR-TB are concerns.
Prevention: BCG, early detection, nutrition (Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana), the National TB Elimination Programme with a goal of ending TB.
Agent: Plasmodium (P. vivax, P. falciparum), transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito; life cycle in mosquito and human liver and red blood cells; fever with chills, anaemia.
Prevention: bed nets, indoor spraying, larvicides, rapid tests and ACT drugs, vaccine R21 in some places; National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016–30).
Surveillance, early treatment, community participation (ASHA), sanitation and vector control, research and antimicrobial resistance monitoring.

conclusion: Both diseases can be controlled by early diagnosis, complete treatment and prevention at community level. Elimination needs sustained funding and attention to the poorest.
